exp.0:1:
He says that God calls all the peoples and the whole earth to listen. The Lord himself, from his holy temple, will be a witness against them. Here "witness" means someone who declares the truth in a trial.

The prophet Micah, from a town called Moresheth, speaks in God's name during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, in Judah. His message concerns Samaria and Jerusalem, and it begins like a summons to a trial. Some understand the "holy temple" to be the temple in Jerusalem, and others understand it to be God's heavenly throne; the text allows both readings.

For today: God sees what we do and is not indifferent. You can ask him to examine your heart with honesty, recognize what you need to correct, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.0:3:
It says that when God shows himself, the whole creation trembles. The mountains melt like wax beside the fire, and the valleys split open like ground that gives way when water rushes down a slope. These are poetic images meant to show God's power; we do not know whether they describe a literal event or are figurative language.

Micah, a prophet from Judah, speaks in the name of the LORD. He calls all the peoples to listen, because God will be a witness against his people. The cause, according to the verses that follow, is the rebellion of Israel and Judah, represented by Samaria and Jerusalem. God comes to judge, not out of whim, but because of their sins.

For today: God is holy and takes sin seriously, but he also warns us in time. Today we can examine our hearts, acknowledge what we have done wrong, and return to him with humility.
exp.1:3:
God says that a day will come when they will be mocked with a proverb and will sing a sad song, like a funeral dirge. They will say: "We are completely ruined. Our land has passed into other hands. God has taken our fields away and given them to others." A proverb is a popular saying, and a lament is a song of sorrow.

The prophet Micah speaks in the name of God. The rich of Judah were seizing the houses and lands of the poor. Now the punishment is coming upon them. It is not entirely clear who sings the lament: it may be the people, or it may be the mockery of their enemies. Many think the invaders would take those lands.

For today: do not take advantage of the weakest to gain more. What is gained through injustice does not last. Be honest in your business and deal fairly with those who depend on you.
exp.1:6:
God asks Israel a strong question, addressing them as the house of Jacob. He asks whether his Spirit has been cut short, that is, whether he has become impatient or powerless. Then he asks whether these threats are the way he acts. And he ends by saying that his words do good to the one who walks uprightly, that is, to the one who lives righteously.

Micah prophesies in a time of injustice. The powerful ask the prophets to be silent and not to speak of judgment or shame. God answers through the prophet: it is not he who has changed, but the people, who reject correction. The verses that follow show their abuses against the weakest.

For today: sometimes we do not want to hear the Word because it makes us uncomfortable. But if we receive it with humility, it does us good and guides us. Ask God for a heart willing to listen, even when you are corrected.
exp.2:1:
It says that Israel's leaders had their values turned upside down: they hated what is good and loved what is evil. Then it uses a strong image: they tear the skin and flesh off the people, as if they were animals. It is figurative language describing abuse, injustice, and the exploitation of the people.

The prophet Micah speaks in God's name to the leaders and rulers of Israel. They were supposed to know and practice justice, but they used it to take advantage of the weakest. That is why God confronts them firmly and warns that there will be consequences.

For today: if we have any kind of authority, at home, at work, or in the church, we should use it to care for others and not to gain an advantage. Let us ask God for a heart that loves what is good and acts with justice.
exp.2:3:
It says that a time will come when unjust leaders will cry out to God for help, but he will not answer them. "Hide his face" means that God turns away and does not show them his favor. The reason is clear: their deeds were evil.

The prophet Micah speaks in the name of God. The rulers and leaders of Judah were abusing the people with violence and injustice, and the prophet uses the image of someone who strips off skin and cuts up meat to describe their cruelty. Then God also rebukes the false prophets who said whatever suited the one paying them.

For today: God invites us to turn back to him while there is still time. Let us not wait until we are in trouble to seek him. If we have harmed others, let us acknowledge it, change our course, and deal justly with those who depend on us.
exp.2:7:
Micah says that he is full of the power of the Spirit of the Lord, along with justice and courage. With that, he can speak clearly to Jacob and Israel, that is, to the people of God, about their rebellion and their sin.

The prophet Micah speaks. Before this, he denounced false prophets who said what the people wanted to hear, and for that reason God would take away all their vision and answer. Micah stands in contrast to them: his message does not come from his own mood or convenience, but from God. Next, he directs his words to the leaders who pervert justice.

For today: if God calls us to speak a difficult truth, we should first seek his Spirit, and speak with courage, justice and love, without adapting the message to please everyone.
exp.3:0:
In the last days, the verse announces, the mountain where the temple of the Lord stands will be the most important place of all. The phrase "in the last days" refers to the future days that God has prepared, and the mountain will be raised above the others, while the hills rise lower than it. Peoples from many nations will come to it.

Micah was a prophet in Judah, around the eighth century B.C. Before this passage he had announced judgment on Jerusalem because of its injustice. Here, God gives hope: after the punishment will come a time of peace, when the nations will learn his ways. Christians often see in this passage Christ and his kingdom; others understand it as something still to be fulfilled.

For today: even when the world lives in conflict, God has an end of peace and justice. That hope invites us to seek his teaching and to be people who promote peace.
exp.3:1:
In the last days, many peoples will come, wanting to know God. They will urge one another, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob." They want him to teach them his ways so that they can walk in his paths. God's teaching will go out from Zion, and his word from Jerusalem.

Micah was a prophet who spoke to Judah at a time of injustice, when judgment was close at hand. Yet here he gives a promise of hope: one day God will be acknowledged by all the nations, and his word will bring peace, as the verses that follow show. Some see this fulfilled in Christ and the church, and others also look for it in a time still to come.

For today: if we long for peace, let us begin by listening to God and obeying him. We can open the Bible with humility, asking him to teach us his ways, and then practice one concrete thing he shows us today.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that God himself will be the judge among many peoples and will correct even the powerful nations, including those far away. Then people will turn their weapons into tools for working the land: they will make their swords into hoes (for breaking up the soil) and their spears into pruning hooks (for cutting the grain). There will be no more war or training for war.

Micah, a prophet of Judah in difficult times, announces this promise for the last days. He speaks of a future when nations will go up to Jerusalem to learn God's ways. His message encouraged a people who lived under threat and violence. Christians often see it fulfilled fully in the kingdom of Christ; others see it as a hope still to come.

For today: if we wait for the peace God promises, let us start practicing it. Today you can set aside a weapon of harsh words and use your hands and your tongue to build up.
exp.3:3:
It says that, in the time God promises, each person will live in peace and in safety. To sit under the vine and under the fig tree was a picture of rest, of work well done, and of having what one needs. The phrase about being made afraid is rewritten here: no one will make them afraid, because God himself has said so.

The prophet Micah speaks, and what he announces comes from the LORD. The people were living with injustice and threats of war. Because of this, God promises a future in which the nations learn his ways, lay down their weapons, and live in peace. Many believers see this as a hope that is still waiting to be fully fulfilled.

For today: when fear or uncertainty overwhelms you, remember that God's word is firm. Right now you can seek his peace in prayer and be someone who helps others live without fear.
exp.3:6:
God promises to take the weakest of his people: the one who is lame (the one who walks with difficulty) and the one who has been driven away (the one who had wandered off or was scattered). From them he will form a remnant that will continue to exist, and a strong nation. A remnant that carries on is what is meant here. The LORD will reign in Mount Zion, from now on and forever.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. The people were living under threats, and talk of exile was in the air, that is, of being carried far away from their land. Even so, God promises to gather the wounded and the afflicted. Many Christians see in this a hope that points toward the reign of the Messiah, although interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: if you feel weak, wounded, or far from God, you are not written off. God does not only help the strong, but gathers and strengthens the broken. Come to Him with confidence and rest on His care.
exp.3:8:
This verse asks questions of Jerusalem, pictured as a daughter of Zion, who cries out in anguish like a woman in labor. It asks whether she has no king and no counselor, that is, no one to guide and rule her. A counselor is someone who gives wise advice. The question sounds almost ironic: why all this fear?

Micah speaks on behalf of God to the people of Judah, before the exile in Babylon. He announces that suffering will come: they will leave the city and go to Babylon. But he also promises that there the LORD will deliver them. Some believe the "king" is God himself, who reigns in Zion; others see here a look ahead to the Messiah, mentioned in the next chapter. Both readings have been held.

For today: when fear or pain makes you feel alone, remember that God is still King and Counselor. Before crying out in anguish, pray and trust that He can guide and sustain you, even in difficult times.
exp.3:10:
Many nations, it says, have gathered against Jerusalem (Zion). They want the city to be defiled, that is, dishonored and treated as worthless, and they want to see its fall with their own eyes.

The prophet Micah speaks in God's name to a people who would go through distress and exile. The verses before this one announce that they would be carried away as far as Babylon, but that there God would rescue them. The verses that follow show that the enemies do not understand God's plan, and that he would change the situation. Scholars debate which exact moment the gathering of nations refers to.

For today: when criticism or pressure surrounds you and seems bigger than you are, remember that what you see is not the whole picture. God has purposes that others do not understand. Entrust your situation to him with confidence and wait for his work.
exp.3:11:
They say that the nations that gathered against Zion did not understand what God was doing. They thought they were going to destroy her, but God gathered them like sheaves brought into the threshing floor. A sheaf is a bundle of cut stalks of grain, and the threshing floor is the place where grain was beaten to separate it from the straw.

The prophet Micah speaks on God's behalf to Jerusalem. He announces that suffering will come, even exile to Babylon, but he also promises rescue. The nations believe they will win, but without knowing it they are part of God's plan. Then Zion will be strengthened to thresh them.

For today: when problems seem to have the last word, remember that God sees more than we see. Trust in Him even when you do not understand His purpose, and ask Him for wisdom to wait for His work.
exp.3:12:
Micah says that Zion, called here the daughter of Zion as a beloved people, must rise up and thresh, like an ox treading out the grain on the threshing floor. God promises her strength: horns of iron and hoofs of bronze. With her she will crush many peoples. The word for the plunder, the gain taken by violence, names what is won by force; that spoil and those riches will be dedicated, that is, given over to the Lord, Lord of the whole earth.

The prophet Micah speaks for God. Many nations gather against Jerusalem, wanting to see her defiled, but they do not understand God's plans: He gathers them like sheaves on the threshing floor, ready to be threshed. The language is figurative, and it has been interpreted in different ways: as a near victory, or as a future hope under the Messiah.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by opposition, do not trust in your own strength, but in God, who strengthens His own. And if He gives you any victory or provision, recognize that it comes from Him and use it to honor Him.
exp.4:0:
This verse describes a city surrounded by enemies. The daughter of troops is told to gather herself into groups, perhaps to defend herself or out of distress. "Troops" means armed companies or bands. The enemies have laid siege, and the judge of Israel, that is, its ruler, will be struck with a rod on the cheek, an act of humiliation.

The prophet Micah speaks to a people facing invasion and judgment for their sin. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of Jerusalem or another city, and whether he has Assyria or Babylon in mind. What follows, in verse 2, announces that a ruler will come out of Bethlehem whose origin is from of old, from eternity. For this reason many Christians see here a contrast with Christ.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart and leaders fail, remember that God is still at work. Trust in the King He has promised.
exp.4:2:
He says that God will leave his people in the hands of their enemies for a time, until the woman who is about to give birth has delivered. After that, the rest of the Lord's brothers, those coming from Bethlehem, will join again with the children of Israel.

The prophet Micah speaks to a people under siege and humiliated. He has just announced that a ruler who is eternal will come out of Bethlehem. Many Christians see in the woman who is to give birth Mary and the birth of Jesus, as in Matthew 2. Others also understand her as Zion in labor pains (Micah 4:10). Both readings have been upheld.

When everything seems lost, God has not abandoned his plan. Seasons of waiting and pain can be like childbirth: difficult, but with a promise. Trust today that God keeps his word in his own time, even when it is slow to become visible.
exp.4:3:
The explanation says that the promised ruler from Bethlehem will care for his people like a shepherd. He will guide, feed, and protect them. He will do this with the strength and greatness that come from God. His people will live safely and in peace, and his fame will reach the most distant places on earth.

The prophet Micah spoke around the eighth century before Christ, when Assyria threatened Judah. God promises a king who will come out of the small town of Bethlehem. The New Testament applies this passage to Jesus (Matthew 2:5-6). The verses that follow say that he will be our peace against our enemies. Some scholars also see a near hope for that time, but Christians read it as fulfilled in Christ.

When you feel small or threatened, remember that Jesus cares for you as a good shepherd. Trust in his strength, not your own, and rest in his peace.
exp.4:7:
The remnant of Jacob, that is, the survivors of the people of Israel, says the verse, will be among many nations like a lion among the animals of the forest, or like a young lion among flocks of sheep. When the lion passes through, no one escapes from it.

The prophet Micah speaks in God's name to a people threatened by Assyria. Earlier he spoke of the remnant as refreshing dew; here he describes it as a lion. These are two images of the same promise: God will care for his people and make them strong. Scholars debate whether it refers to the near future or to the time of the Messiah, who is announced in verse 2.

For today: when you feel small or surrounded by pressures, remember that your strength does not come from your own resources, but from God. Trust in him and act with courage and kindness.
exp.4:10:
God says that he will destroy the cities of his people's land and tear down all their strongholds. The "strongholds" are the walled and protected places where people felt safe.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Micah to Israel. In this passage, along with removing horses, chariots, sorcery and idols, God clears away everything the people were placing their trust in instead of in him. Scholars understand it in different ways: some see a judgment that purifies, others a promise for the time of the Messiah. Even so, the central message is that God wants to be the only security of his people.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I rely on more than God, such as money, my job or my plans? Handing those securities over to him gives us a steadier peace.
exp.5:3:
God reminds his people that it was he who brought them up out of Egypt, the land where they lived as slaves. He bought them back, that is, he rescued them and set them free. He also sent three leaders to guide them: Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

God speaks as though bringing a case to court against Israel, and the mountains serve as witnesses. He asks what wrong he has done them, and in answer he recalls his acts of kindness. After this, the people will ask how they can please God with sacrifices, but the prophet will show them what truly matters.

Today we can also remember how God has cared for us, helped us, and guided us, sometimes through specific people. Remembering this leads us to gratitude and to answering him with a faithful life, not only with religious acts.
exp.5:5:
Here someone asks with what they could come before God in order to please him. Calves of a year old were young animals, considered valuable.

God has just reminded his people that he brought them out of Egypt and sent them Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. Then someone from the people responds with questions, perhaps with a tone of complaint or of sincerity. Scholars discuss the exact tone. God's answer comes in verse 8: what he asks for is justice, mercy, and humility, rather than great offerings.

For today: do not try to win God's favor with impressive activities or sacrifices. Come near to him with a humble heart, treat others with justice and compassion, and walk closely with him each day.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that God has already shown people what is good. He does not ask for enormous sacrifices, but for three things: to do justly, which means to act with fairness; to love mercy, that is, to show kindness and compassion toward others; and to walk humbly with God, that is, to live with simplicity and obedience at his side.

Micah was a prophet in Judah. In this passage, God brings a complaint against his people. Someone asks whether he should offer thousands of rams, rivers of oil, and even his firstborn child. The answer is that God does not seek exaggerated rituals, but a just and faithful life. The verses that follow speak of unfair dealings and dishonest measures.

For today: before seeking something grand to impress God, ask yourself how you treat people. Today you can be honest in your work, help someone with patience, and pray with humility.
exp.5:14:
He says the people will work hard, but will not enjoy the fruit of their labor. They will sow and not reap. They will tread the olives, but will not anoint themselves with the oil. They will tread the grapes, but will not drink the wine.

God speaks, through the prophet Micah, in a case against his people. He accuses them of injustice, of cheating in business, and of following wicked customs, like those of Omri and Ahab, kings of Israel known for their evil. These losses are the consequence of their disobedience.

For today: examine whether your way of earning and spending is honest before God. Working hard is not enough; we need to live with justice and humility, trusting that his blessing is worth more than any harvest.
exp.6:1:
It says that good and compassionate people have disappeared from the land. The phrase about the compassionate man being gone means that no one can be found who has mercy. The word for someone upright is someone honest and just. To lie in wait for blood means to watch in ambush in order to do harm, even to kill. To set a net means to lay traps, as people do to catch animals, but here it is against one's own brother.

The prophet Micah speaks, and he does so with pain. He compares himself to a field already harvested, where not a single cluster is left, because he finds almost no one faithful to God. He describes a corrupt society, with judges and rulers who let themselves be bought. Then he announces that God will intervene and call them to account. Micah does not stay with mere complaint, for in verse 7 he says he will wait for God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are people of mercy and honesty in our work, our families, and our church. Even though deception abounds around us, we can treat others with justice and kindness, and trust that God sees everything.
exp.6:3:
Even the best of the people are harmful, the explanation says, like the buckthorn and the bramble, prickly bushes that wound anyone who comes near. The watchmen are the prophets who kept guard and gave warning. The day of visitation is the day when God steps in to judge. Then the people will be thrown into confusion, that is, disturbed and not knowing what to do.

The prophet Micah speaks in the eighth century B.C., lamenting the corruption of Judah: judges who are bought, abusive leaders, and betrayal even among family members. He sees that the warning of the prophets will be fulfilled. Some understand the phrase "your visitation" as directed at the people, while others see it as a general announcement of God's judgment.

For today: do not be discouraged by injustice, and do not become cynical. Examine your own heart, be honest and merciful wherever you are, and trust that God sees and will act with justice.
exp.6:5:
It says that corruption has reached families: sons show no respect for their fathers, and daughters and daughters-in-law rise against their mothers and mothers-in-law. A person's worst enemies would be those of his own household.

The prophet Micah speaks here, lamenting the state of the people of Israel. No one can be trusted anymore: not friends, not leaders, not even one's wife. The thorny plants mentioned show that even the best can hurt. But he does not stop at complaint: in verse 7 he chooses to wait upon God. Jesus quoted this verse in Matthew 10:35-36 when speaking of the divisions that come from following his way.

For today: if there is tension or pain in your family, do not lose heart. Bring it to God in prayer, seek peace with wisdom, and place your hope in Him, who hears you.
exp.6:6:
It says that, even though everything around the speaker fails, he will place his trust in the LORD. The verse's "I will wait" means to wait patiently and in faith. The word "salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not merely good physical condition. The prophet affirms that God will hear him when he cries out.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of the faithful people, in a time of great corruption. The verses before describe betrayal even within the family. The verses that follow show that the speaker acknowledges his sin, accepts God's discipline, and trusts that God will raise him up. Scholars debate which exact period the passage reflects, but the message of hope is clear.

For today: when people disappoint you, do not let bitterness have the last word. Bring your pain to God in prayer and wait for Him with patience, knowing that He hears you.
exp.6:9:
Here the text says that the enemy woman who mocked, asking "Where is the Lord your God?", will see that God does act, and she will be put to shame. Being trampled down means being crushed underfoot, and the mud of the streets shows a complete and humiliating fall.

The people of Israel are speaking, represented as a voice that confesses its sin but waits on God. It had suffered punishment and mockery from an enemy nation. It is not stated with certainty which nation is meant; some think of Assyria or Babylon, and others see it in a more general way. The hope is that God will defend his own after correcting them.

For today: when you feel weak or are mocked for your faith, you do not have to take revenge or despair. Acknowledge your failures honestly, trust that God is your light in the darkness, and wait patiently for his justice.
exp.6:15:
The explanation says that the nations, when they see the wonders God will do for his people, will be put to shame for the power they once boasted of. In the verse, "all their might" stands in for the strength they relied on. To lay the hand upon the mouth is to be left without words, silent and amazed. The phrase about the ears can be understood as not wanting to hear any more, or as being stunned before the power of God.

Micah, the prophet, has been praying that God would care for his people like a shepherd. God answers by promising wonders like those of the going out from Egypt. Israel was weak and humbled, and this promise gave it back its hope. The verses that follow show that the nations will fear God, and then the prophet praises his forgiveness and his mercy.

For today: when you feel small before problems or powerful people, remember that human strength has limits, but God does not. Trust that he cares for his own and acts with justice and mercy.
exp.6:16:
The explanation says that the nations that once thought themselves strong will be humbled, crawling and licking the dust like a serpent. They will come trembling out of their hiding places, that is, their shelters or strongholds. Their fear will be like that of creeping things that come out of the earth. They will fear the Lord our God, and stand in awe before his people.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of God's people, after a time of judgment and pain. God promises wonders like those at the going out from Egypt. Some understand that the nations will truly surrender, and others that they will only be afraid. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when evil seems greater than God, remember that no human power has the last word. Trust in Him, and let his mercy, not your pride, be your refuge.
exp.6:19:
He says that God will fulfill what he promised. Giving means that you will grant or bestow something on someone. Here, faithfulness means that God is firm and trustworthy. Mercy is his loyal and compassionate love. God swore these promises to Abraham, to Jacob, and to their descendants a very long time ago.

Micah, a prophet of Israel, ends his book with this song of praise. The people had been judged for their sin, but the prophet trusts that God will restore them. His hope is not that the people deserve it, but that God is faithful to his covenant.

For today: when you feel unworthy because of your failures, remember that God does not accept you based on your performance, but on his faithfulness and his mercy. Return to him with confidence, ask for forgiveness, and rest in the knowledge that he keeps what he promises.
exp.4:8:
He says God promises victory to his people over those who attack them. "Your hand will be lifted over your foes" speaks of power and triumph. The phrase "cut off" is the key word here, meaning removed or eliminated, the way a tree is cut down.

Micah prophesied to Judah when nations were threatening it. Here God speaks through the prophet and addresses the faithful remnant of Jacob, the group that survives. Earlier he compared them to dew that blesses and to a strong lion. Then he says he will remove horses, chariots, and fortresses, meaning the people's trust will not be placed in weapons. Interpreters debate whether this refers to a near time or to the future of the Messiah.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, do not place your security in your own resources. Trust in God, who cares for his own and is the one who gives the final victory.
exp.6:0:
The prophet cries out in deep sorrow. He feels like someone who comes to the field after the harvest is over: the summer fruit has already been picked, the vines have already been searched, and not a single cluster is left to eat. In his reader's verse the picture is of one gathering summer fruit after the harvest, going through the vineyard for whatever remains. He was hungry for the early fig he longed for, the best and most desired fruit, and none was there.

The speaker is the prophet Micah. With this picture he expresses his sadness at seeing that among his people there are almost no good or faithful people left. The verses that follow describe violence, deceit, and judges who can be bought. The empty field represents a society without goodness.

For today: do not get used to injustice or let it pass by. You can bring your sorrow honestly to God, as Micah did, and ask him to help you be, even in small ways, a faithful and just person.
exp.5:6:
Here someone asks whether the Lord would be pleased with a huge amount: thousands of rams or ten thousand rivers of oil, the kinds of offerings brought to the temple. Then the speaker goes further and asks whether they should give their firstborn child for their wrongdoing. "Transgression" means going against God, and "the fruit of my body" is their child.

Micah presents God bringing his people to trial. The one speaking is a person who wants to be right with God and keeps raising the price of what they would offer. The question is rhetorical: the answer is that God does not look for that. Verse 8 makes it clear: he asks for justice, mercy, and humility. The sacrifice of children was practiced by neighboring peoples and was condemned in God's law.

Today we may think God can be won over with effort, service, or money. He asks for a sincere heart. Before doing something great for God, ask yourself: am I treating those around me with justice and kindness, and walking humbly with Him?
exp.5:8:
The LORD calls out to the city. A wise person will take seriously God's name, that is, who He is and what He says. The word "heed" means to listen and pay attention. The "rod" is the punishment or correction, and "the One who ordained it" is God Himself, who allows it or sends it.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. He has just said that He does not want only sacrifices, but justice, mercy, and humility. Then he denounces the city's dishonest business dealings. Some believe this refers to Jerusalem; the Hebrew text of this phrase is difficult and is translated in several ways.

Today: if God corrects you, do not harden your heart. Listen, examine your life, especially your honesty at work and with money, and return to Him with humility.
exp.5:2:
God asks his people, "My people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Testify against Me." Then he invites them to answer and accuse him, if they can. To weary someone means to tire them out or weigh them down with a heavy demand.

The LORD speaks, and the prophet Micah presents the scene as a court case, with the mountains as witnesses. God does not speak like a tyrant, but like someone who has been hurt and wants to speak with clarity. Right away he reminds them how he delivered them from Egypt and sent them Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. His past faithfulness contrasts with the people's ingratitude.

For today: when you drift away from God or doubt him, remember what he has done for you. Speak with God honestly, and remember that he seeks us out with love, not with contempt.
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces the book. It says that what follows is "the word of the LORD," meaning a message that comes from God, and that it came to Micah, a man from Moresheth. It names three kings of Judah: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The phrase "that came to Micah" means it reached him. The words "what he saw" refer to a vision or revelation about Samaria and Jerusalem.

Micah is the prophet who speaks, but he makes clear that the message is not his own. The three kings show that he ministered over a long period, roughly in the eighth century B.C. Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom and Jerusalem of the southern kingdom. Both cities will receive God's warning for their sin, as will be seen later.

For today: before offering your opinion, listen to what God says in his Word. Read it with humility, knowing that God speaks truly about people, about cities, and also about you.
exp.1:1:
These people want other people's fields and houses, and they seize them by force. They long for what belongs to someone else and take it. Their greed leads them to harm the man himself, his home, and his property. The word "inheritance" in this verse refers to the land a family received as its share, passed down through generations.

Micah is a prophet who speaks for God in Judah, around the eighth century B.C. Just before this verse, he condemns people who plan wrongdoing while lying in bed and carry it out as soon as morning comes, because they have the power to do it. In Israel, the land was given by God to each family, so taking it was a grave injustice. That is why God announces a punishment.

For today: let us examine whether we take advantage of someone weaker, whether at work, in business, or in the family. Let us seek to be just and to defend those who have no power.
exp.0:4:
God's judgment, described in the previous verse with mountains melting away, comes because of the sin of his people. God asks where the rebellion of Jacob began, that is, the northern kingdom, and answers: Samaria, its capital. The "high places" were the raised sites where idolatry was practiced; in Judah, the southern kingdom, the center of the problem was Jerusalem.

Micah, a prophet from Judah, speaks in God's name. Samaria and Jerusalem were the capitals, and from them leaders led the people into idolatry and injustice. That is why the message points first to the center, not only to the outlying areas.

For today: sin is not dealt with by blaming only others; it is wise to ask ourselves what the root is in our own hearts and in our homes. Those who have influence, such as parents or leaders, must take care with their example, and all of us can return to God with humility.
exp.0:15:
It says that someone should shave their head as a sign of mourning. Tearing out your hair and cutting it very close to the scalp were both ways of showing grief. "Your precious children" are the beloved children, the ones who brought joy. The phrase about making yourselves as bald as an eagle probably refers to the vulture, which has an almost bare head. The reason: those children will be taken far away, into exile.

The prophet Micah speaks, in the name of God, to the people of Judah (many think he is addressing Jerusalem or its towns). The verses before it mention several towns near Gath, with wordplays in Hebrew. God announces judgment for the people's sin: an invasion would come and the people would be carried into exile. The exact historical details are debated.

For today: do not minimize the pain that the consequences of sin bring, or the losses that follow. Bring your sorrow to God honestly, ask for a humble heart that repents in time, and trust that He remains faithful and compassionate.
exp.6:2:
Their leaders are skilled at doing evil, and they put great effort into it. The prince and the judge demand a bribe, and the powerful man openly voices his corrupt desires. Together they conspire to bring it about and seal the deal among themselves.

The prophet Micah speaks with grief. He looks at his nation like a field already harvested, with no good fruit left. Almost no honest people remain, and the corruption reaches even those who should guard justice. Then he announces that God will come to call them to account.

For today: do not grow used to injustice or approve of it with your silence. Be honest in small things, refuse bribes, and pray for those who govern, trusting that God sees and will do justice.
exp.6:7:
The explanation says that the speaker addresses an enemy and asks him not to gloat over his fall. Although he has fallen, he will get up again; although he sits in darkness, the LORD will be his light. "Do not gloat over me" means "do not rejoice or mock at my misfortune." "The LORD" is the name of God.

The prophet Micah speaks here on behalf of God's people. Earlier he described a corrupt society, with betrayal even within families. Afterward he acknowledges that the punishment came because of sin, but he trusts that God will defend his cause. Who exactly the "enemy" is has been understood in several ways: a neighboring nation, or the enemies of the people in general.

For today: when you fail or go through a dark time, do not stay on the ground. Acknowledge your mistake, wait on God, and rise up trusting that He will guide you.
exp.6:4:
It says that one can no longer rely on a friend or put trust in a companion. For that reason the text advises guarding what you say. "Seal the doors of your mouth" means "watch yourself" and "be careful what you say," especially with the one who lies in your arms. A "prince" is a ruler or chief.

The prophet Micah speaks, and he does so with sadness. He describes a people where judges are bought, the powerful do as they please, and families are divided. It is a picture of general corruption. The verses that follow say that he looks to the Lord and waits for God, his savior.

Today we can learn that, when people fail, God remains faithful. If someone has betrayed you, do not let bitterness take control. Be wise about what you share, and seek God's help first in prayer.
exp.4:1:
He says that Bethlehem Ephrathah, though it is small among the clans of Judah, will be the place from which a ruler for Israel will come. The phrase "clans of Judah" refers to the family groups that made up the tribe. The ruler's origins are "of old, from the days of eternity," meaning he has existed from ancient times, beyond any beginning.

The prophet Micah is speaking. Israel was going through a crisis: the verse before describes an enemy siege and a judge struck on the cheek with a rod. Against that picture of defeat, God promises a different kind of king. Christians see here a prophecy of Jesus, and Matthew 2:5-6 quotes this passage. Some scholars also see an earlier meaning in the line of David, who came from Bethlehem.

For today: God often works through what is small and what seems insignificant. If you feel unimportant or are in the middle of a crisis, trust that He can carry out His plans with you and through you.
exp.0:6:
God says that Samaria will be completely destroyed. Its carved images will be smashed to pieces, its wages will be burned in the fire, and all its idols will be left in ruins. "Carved images" refers to idols made by hand; "wages" are what she collected, here tied to her spiritual unfaithfulness. Since she collected the wages of a prostitute, those same riches will be carried off and used again in the same way by others. What she gained through her unfaithfulness will return to those who take it.

God speaks through the prophet Micah in the 8th century B.C. He accuses Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, of rebelling against Him and worshipping idols. Many understand "the wages of a prostitute" to refer to wealth tied to pagan worship, though some also think of payments from alliances with other nations. The text does not fully specify this.

For today: examine what things in your heart occupy the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. What is built far from Him does not last. Return to God with sincerity.
exp.5:4:
God tells his people to remember what Balak, king of Moab, planned and what Balaam, son of Beor, answered him. He also points to the journey "from Shittim to Gilgal," so that they would come to recognize the righteousness of the LORD. Here, "righteousness" refers to the just and faithful things the LORD has done for his people.

God speaks through the prophet Micah in a kind of legal case against Israel. God reminds them how he rescued them from Egypt. According to Numbers 22 to 24, Balak wanted Balaam to curse Israel, but God did not allow it. Shittim and Gilgal mark the final stretch of the crossing into the promised land, although scholars explain this in several ways.

When we feel far from God or doubt his care, it helps us to remember the times he protected and sustained us. Remembering his faithfulness awakens gratitude and encourages us to live with sincere obedience.
exp.4:11:
God says he will cut away the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers. That is, he will remove the practices of seeking power or answers through hidden means, and the people who claimed to foretell the future by reading signs.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Micah. In this passage he announces a purification of his people "in that day." He removes the horses, the chariots, the fortresses, the idols, and the sorceries, which were things Israel trusted in instead of trusting God. Scholars understand this as a cleansing meant to restore, though not all agree on how it is fulfilled.

For today: ask yourself where you seek security or answers apart from God. It may be horoscopes, money, or the need to control everything. Surrender that trust to him in prayer, and allow him to remove what pulls you away from him.
exp.2:9:
The explanation says that Israel's leaders were building up the city of Zion, which is Jerusalem, through violence and injustice. "Build" is the word that matters here, meaning to construct, and "bloodshed" speaks of crimes and of lives crushed in order to get rich. "Jerusalem" is the city's name as it appears in the Bible.

The prophet Micah speaks, filled with the Spirit of the LORD, and addresses the heads, judges, priests, and prophets. They accepted bribes, sold their teaching, and yet still said, "The LORD is among us." Because of this, Micah announces that Jerusalem would be plowed like a field. Scholars do not agree on which specific abuse he had in mind, but the underlying sin is clear.

For today: our achievements, businesses, or ministries do not please God if they are built on abuse or injustice. Today we can examine how we treat those who depend on us, and seek to prosper with honesty and justice.
exp.4:5:
The explanation says that God's people, under the leadership of the promised shepherd, will defeat their enemy. The verse says they will rule over the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod with the blade drawn. "Assyria" is Assyria, and "the land of Nimrod" is another way of naming that same region. The phrase "marches into our borders" means that the invader steps across our frontiers. God will deliver us when Assyria invades our land.

The prophet Micah speaks in a time when Assyria threatened both Israel and Judah. This comes from the promise of the ruler born in Bethlehem (5:2), whose coming is described as bringing peace. Many Christians see Christ here; Assyria may also represent God's enemies in general. Interpreters debate the details.

For today: when you feel that something stronger than you is threatening you, trust that Christ, the good shepherd, cares for his own. Pray and act with courage, without despair.
exp.5:11:
The verse says that the wealthy people of the city were full of violence, and that the residents spoke lies, with deceit in their mouths. "Full of violence" means the violence was widespread and complete. "Violence" here is harm and oppression carried out by force against others. "Residents" are the people who live in the city. The phrase "their tongues are deceitful in their mouths" describes speech full of trickery that had become a habit.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. He has just accused the people of using false weights and dishonest measures in trade. Here he shows that the injustice was not limited to a few, but had become part of everyday life. That is why, in the verses that follow, he announces consequences: scarcity, loss, and frustration.

For today: God is concerned with honesty in everyday life, such as work, prices, contracts, and words. Today we can examine whether we are fair in our accounts, promises, and dealings, even when no one sees us.
exp.0:2:
God says he comes forth from his dwelling place, that is, from his heavenly home, and comes down to the earth. "Tread on" means to step on with force, and the "high places" are the mountains and elevated ground. It is a poetic picture of God coming as judge, with power and authority over all creation.

Micah was a prophet from Judah who spoke in the days of the kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. God sent him with a message for Samaria and Jerusalem. The verses that follow explain the reason: the rebellion and sin of the people. The high places were also sites where idolatry was practiced, so some see here a judgment on those false places. This latter point is one possible interpretation, not something the text states directly.

God is not indifferent to sin. Today we can examine our hearts with sincerity and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.0:12:
The verse tells the people of Lachish to harness their chariot horses, which means get ready to flee. It also says that Lachish was the starting point of sin for Jerusalem, called the Daughter of Zion, and that Israel's rebellions were found there.

The prophet Micah speaks for God to cities of Judah that were threatened by an invasion. Lachish was a fortified city. Scholars are not certain what its sin was: some think it was idolatry, and others think it was trusting in chariots and horses instead of God. In the original Hebrew there is a wordplay on the name Lachish and the word for swift horse.

Today, it is worth asking ourselves what we truly trust in: our own resources or God. We should also take care that our bad example does not become the starting point of harm for others.
exp.6:10:
The verse says that a day will come when the walls will be rebuilt, and on that same day the boundary will be extended. The word translated "boundary" is hard to pin down: it can mean a decree, a fixed limit, or the border of a territory. Some take it as a limit that is pushed outward, so that the people's land grows; others take it as the boundary that is enlarged or redrawn. The Hebrew allows more than one reading.

Micah speaks on behalf of a people who have turned back to God. He admits their wrongdoing, accepts the discipline they have received, and confidently expects that God will defend and restore them. This verse announces hope after judgment.

For today: even when you are living with the consequences of your mistakes, God does not leave you there. Admit your failure honestly, trust in Him, and wait for His restoration, because He knows how to rebuild what has fallen.
exp.0:11:
The people of Maroth ache and wait for something good, but calamity instead comes to them. "Dwellers" means the people who live there, that is, the townsfolk. "Maroth" sounds similar to the Hebrew word for "bitterness," and many believe Micah is playing on that meaning. The calamity that comes from the LORD is a judgment that reaches even to the gate of Jerusalem.

The prophet Micah speaks in the eighth century before Christ. He laments the judgment coming upon Judah because of its sin and idolatry. He lists towns near Jerusalem with wordplays in Hebrew. It is understood that the enemy advance, probably Assyrian, would come closer and closer. The exact details of Maroth are uncertain.

For today: God does not ignore sin, but He warns before He acts. If we feel His call to change, let us not wait until the problem reaches the gate. Today we can repent and return to Him, who forgives with great mercy.
exp.1:8:
God accuses the powerful among his people of mistreating the women, driving them out of their homes, which were places of rest and joy. He also takes away from the children what he calls "my blessing," that is, the honor and favor God had given them, and which was meant to last forever.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. In these chapters he denounces those who plan wrong and seize the fields, houses, and clothing of the weakest. Here the harm reaches widows and orphans, who are left without a home and without protection. The exact details of these events are not known to us, but God's complaint is clear: his people had become enemies of their own neighbors.

For today: God looks out for those who are left unprotected. Ask yourself whom you can care for, defend, or help, and avoid taking advantage of your position to harm others. May your home and your dealings protect the dignity of the most vulnerable.
exp.6:17:
There is no god like You, because You pardon wickedness and pass over the sin of those who remain as Your people. The phrase "inheritance" refers to the people God regards as His own. "Delights in loving devotion" means that God takes pleasure in showing faithful love, and His anger does not last forever.

The prophet Micah speaks here at the end of his book. After describing judgment and grief over Israel's sin, he closes by praising God. The verses that follow say that God will again show mercy and will cast their sins into the depths of the sea, according to his promise to Abraham and Jacob.

If you feel guilty about something, bring it honestly to God. He does not tire of forgiving the one who returns to Him. Rest in that mercy, and try to show that same faithful love to those who have failed you.
exp.6:11:
On that day, the explanation says, people from many places will return to Israel: from Assyria, from the cities of Egypt, from Egypt all the way to the Euphrates River, and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. The image is of a wide gathering, with people coming from every direction.

The prophet Micah speaks, and in this passage he addresses Zion, the city of God. He has just expressed his hope in God in the middle of judgment. Interpreters differ: some see here the return of the scattered Israelites, while others see the arrival of peoples from many nations. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: when you feel that everything in your life is scattered or broken, remember that God knows how to gather and restore. Wait on Him with patience and keep trusting, even when you do not yet see the change.
exp.0:7:
Micah says that he will weep and cry out in grief over what is coming. He will walk barefoot and naked, that is, without his normal clothing and shoes, as was done as a sign of mourning. His crying will be like the howling of jackals and the mourning of ostriches, animals whose sounds are sad and lonely.

The one speaking is the prophet Micah, though his words express the grief of God over the judgment announced against Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, because of its idolatry. Some think Micah actually walked this way as a symbolic sign; others believe it is a poetic way of expressing his sorrow. The text does not make this entirely clear. What is clear is that the prophet takes no pleasure in the punishment.

Today we can learn to feel sorrow over sin and its consequences, rather than judging coldly or with pride. Let us ask God for a tender heart, one that prays and weeps for those who turn away from Him.
exp.3:7:
He says God is speaking to Jerusalem, called the "watchtower of the flock," like a tower where the sheep are watched over. He promises that the former dominion will be restored to it. "Former dominion" means the rule and authority the city once held, and "Daughter of Zion" is a poetic way of naming the people of Jerusalem.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of the LORD. The people lived under threat and would be carried off to Babylon, as the following verses say. God assures them that their fall will not be the end: there will be restoration. Some Christians see here a sign of the reign of the Messiah; others connect it more closely to the return from exile. Both readings have been held.

For today: when you feel you have lost everything, remember that God can restore what seems finished. Trust in Him, even if the road first passes through hard moments.
exp.5:15:
The verse says that the people have kept the statutes of Omri and followed the practices of Ahab's house, and have obeyed their counsel. Because of this, God will turn them into a desolation, which means total ruin, and their inhabitants will become an object of contempt, people others look at with scorn. They will bear the scorn of the nations.

God speaks through the prophet Micah and brings His complaint against His people. Omri and Ahab were kings of Israel whom the Bible remembers for their wickedness and idolatry (1 Kings 16 and 21). God had already said that their injustices, such as deceit and violence, would bring scarcity and loss. This verse names the cause: following bad examples.

For today: let us think about whom we are imitating. Customs, fashions, or advice can pull us away from God without our noticing. Let us measure each path against what God asks: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with Him (Micah 6:8).
exp.0:13:
It says that Judah will have to send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath, the way a family sends a daughter off with gifts when she leaves home to be married. In other words, Judah will hand that town over to the invaders. Then it says that the houses of Achzib will prove deceptive to the kings of Israel. The name Achzib sounds like a Hebrew word meaning deceit or something that fails. The town looked like it would offer help, but it will not deliver it.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of God to the towns of Judah as the Assyrian army advances. He uses wordplay with the names of the towns. God warns that sin brings consequences, and that human allies and defenses will fail.

For today: do not put your security in things that seem firm but can fail, such as money, connections, or your own strength. Seek God with humility, turn back from wrongdoing in time, and trust the One who never deceives.
exp.6:8:
The speaker says he knows he has sinned against God and that, for this reason, he will patiently accept God's discipline. Yet he trusts that God, in the end, will take up his cause and bring about justice. "I must endure" means to put up with the hardship without giving up; "until He argues my case" means that God will plead on his behalf; "He will bring me into the light" means that God will lead him out of darkness into freedom.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of God's people in a time of downfall and mockery by their enemies. Some understand it to be the voice of a repentant Judah or Jerusalem. It does not claim that their suffering is unjust, but accepts it as the consequence of their sin, while hoping that God will restore them.

When we fail, we can be honest with God, without excuses or despair. His correction is not the end: if we return to Him, He lifts us up and restores our hope.
exp.4:13:
God says he will pull up the Asherah poles, which were wooden posts or sacred trees used to worship false gods, probably the goddess Asherah. He also says he will demolish your cities. Some scholars believe the cities may be fortified ones, while others think the words speak of idols or enemies. It is not entirely certain.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. After promising a ruler who would be born in Bethlehem, he announces that he will cleanse his people of idolatry, witchcraft, and trust in their own strength, so that they depend on him alone.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: money, success, superstitions, or our own plans. Ask God to show you what you need to remove from your life, and trust in him again.
exp.0:5:
He says God will turn Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, into a heap of rubble in the open field, a place where vines are planted. Its stones will be poured down into the valley, and its foundations will be exposed, that is, the base on which its buildings once stood.

God speaks through the prophet Micah in the eighth century B.C. Samaria had fallen into idolatry and injustice, and for this reason it receives this judgment. Afterward Samaria was conquered by Assyria, something history confirms. Micah also warns that Jerusalem is guilty as well.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he warns us so that we will turn back to him. We can ask him to show us which idols have taken his place in our hearts, and return to him with humility.
exp.1:4:
They say that those who took land from others will no longer have a share in the division among God's people. Dividing the land by lot meant measuring out a piece of land with a measuring line and assigning the portions to families by lot. "The assembly of the LORD" is the gathering of the people of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. The wealthy people of Judah plotted evil and seized the fields and houses of others (vv. 1-2). God answers that the same judgment will take away their place. The land was an inheritance given by God to each family, so losing it meant losing one's place among the people. Some explain the verse as the end of any future division of land, and others as an immediate loss; the general meaning is the same.

For today: God sees how we treat the weak. Examine whether, in your work or business, you take advantage of other people's need, and choose to act with justice and honesty.
exp.5:13:
God announces a punishment in four images. They will eat, but will stay hungry. Your hunger will remain inside you, so that even a full meal leaves you empty. You will try to gather and hold on to things to keep them safe, but you will not succeed. And whatever little you manage to save, God says he will hand over to the sword, that is, to war and destruction.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Micah, addressing the city of Jerusalem or Samaria, depending on how one interprets it. The rich had filled themselves with robbery and lies. That is why God disciplines them. The following verses say they followed the evil practices of Omri and Ahab, unjust kings.

For today: Wealth gained through deceit never truly satisfies. Today we can ask ourselves whether our work and our earnings are honest, and ask God to teach us to live justly and to trust in his provision.
exp.2:8:
Here the prophet speaks directly to the leaders of the people: the "leaders of the house of Jacob" and the "rulers of the house of Israel." These were the chiefs, judges, and those in charge. He charges them with despising justice and perverting all that is right, meaning they hate what is fair and bend what is right to suit themselves.

Micah speaks as one moved by the Spirit of the LORD to confront the sin of his people. The leaders were meant to look after the people with justice, but they used their power for their own gain. The verses that follow show that they accepted bribes and still believed God would protect them.

For today: if you have any authority, at home, at work, or in the church, use it with honesty and fair treatment. Ask God to help you not to bend what is right for money, comfort, or fear.
exp.1:0:
This verse is a "woe," a warning spoken with sorrow and anger. It speaks of people who lie awake at night plotting evil instead of resting. "Iniquity" means injustice and wickedness. When morning comes, they carry out what they planned, because the power to do it is in their hands.

Micah was a prophet who spoke in God's name to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, probably in the eighth century B.C. The verses that follow explain the problem: some powerful people were taking fields and houses away from ordinary, humble people. God says he sees that injustice and that there will be consequences.

For today: let us be careful about what we plan in secret. If we have any power, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, let us ask God to help us use it to serve others and not to take advantage of them.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the faithful remnant of Jacob's people, meaning the survivors of Israel, will be among many nations like dew from the LORD and like showers on the grass. "Remnant" means those who are left. The wording about people waiting or lingering refers to humans. Dew and rain do not depend on anyone; they come from God.

The prophet Micah speaks to Israel in a time of threat from Assyria. He has just announced a ruler who will bring peace, and he promises that God will deliver his people. Here the remnant is a blessing, like water that refreshes. The next verse compares it to a lion, showing another side of its strength. Some see in this a promise for Israel of that time, and others also see a promise for the future.

For today: you do not need anyone's approval to be a blessing to others. If God sustains you, you can refresh others with kindness, even in difficult surroundings.
exp.6:14:
God promises his people that he will once again do great miracles, like the ones he performed when he brought them out of slavery in Egypt. "My wonders" are astonishing works that only God can do.

Here God is speaking, answering the prophet's prayer in the previous verse, where Micah asks him to care for his people as a shepherd cares for his flock. Israel was living through a time of great corruption and judgment, but God answers with hope. Scholars understand in different ways when and how this promise is fulfilled, but the central message is clear: God does not abandon his own.

For today: when your situation seems hopeless, remember what God has already done in the past. That remembrance helps you wait with confidence that he can act again.
exp.0:14:
God says he will bring a conqueror against Mareshah, someone who will take possession of the city, probably an invader who will overrun it. "The glory of Israel" refers to the leaders and nobles of Judah, who will flee as far as Adullam, a cave or stronghold where they used to hide. There is a wordplay here: Mareshah sounds similar to the word for "possessor" or "conqueror."

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of God. He announces judgment on the cities of Judah for their sin and idolatry. Many understand this as referring to the Assyrian invasion, although the details for each city are interpreted in various ways. The "glory" of Israel ends up humbled and hidden.

For today: let us not trust in our prestige or in our sense of security. If we have neglected God, it is better to turn back to him with humility before everything collapses, for he is merciful to those who repent.
exp.3:4:
Micah 4:5 says that, though all the nations may walk in the names of their gods, God's people choose to walk in the name of the LORD their God forever and ever. The verse sets two ways of living side by side, with the faithful people choosing their own path with the LORD.

Micah was a prophet in Judah about 2,700 years ago. Just before this verse he describes a future of peace, when God will judge between the peoples and there will be no more war. This verse shows the response of the faithful people: not waiting for everything to change, but deciding from now on to follow God. Afterward, God promises to gather the weak and the scattered.

For today: even though many around you live without God or follow other things, you can decide today to walk with Him in everyday life: in your work, your family and your decisions, through prayer and obedience.
exp.5:10:
Does God ask whether he can excuse someone who uses dishonest scales and carries a bag of false weights? The question is rhetorical: the answer is no. To "excuse" here means to overlook or pardon. The "weights" were stones or pieces of metal placed on the scale to measure money or goods.

Here God himself speaks, calling the city through the prophet Micah. He is bringing a charge against his people. The verses around it say that the rich have filled themselves with violence and lies. For God, cheating in business is not a minor detail but an injustice that harms the poor.

For today: check your own scales. Be honest when you sell, charge, pay, and work, even when no one is watching. God cares about integrity in everyday life.
exp.5:0:
God says to listen to his word. He asks someone, in this case the prophet, to stand up and present a case, as in a court, before the mountains and the hills. "Plead" means to argue or defend a cause in a court of law. "Hear" is the word for listening. The mountains are to serve as witnesses who listen.

The one speaking is the Lord through the prophet Micah. In the verses that follow, God says he has a dispute with his people, Israel. He calls the mountains and the foundations of the earth as witnesses, because they are firm and have been there from the beginning. Then he asks with sorrow: "What have I done to you?" God does not act like a tyrant, but listens and wants to restore the relationship.

For today: when you feel yourself drifting away from God, do not run. He invites you to speak honestly, and also to listen humbly to what he says to you.
exp.2:5:
The passage says that a spiritual night will come upon the false prophets. They will receive no visions and will be unable to divine. It is as if the sun were setting on them and the daylight were turning black over them. Divining here refers to the supposed revelations they once claimed to give. The reader sees the word "divination" in the verse above, and that is the practice being described.

God speaks through Micah. These prophets would speak of peace to those who paid them, and they would declare war on anyone who did not feed them. They preached for their own gain, not according to the truth. For this reason God takes away all revelation from them, and they are put to shame because they have no answer from God.

For today: examine whom you listen to and why. Seek out voices that speak God's truth even when it is uncomfortable, not only what pleases the ear. And when you speak of God, do so with honesty, without seeking personal advantage.
exp.4:14:
God says he will act with intense anger and bring justice against the nations that refused to obey him. Here "vengeance" means justice that corrects and punishes wrongdoing. "Wrath" is a very strong anger. "Nations" means peoples or nations.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. Just before this, he announces that he will remove the idols, the images, and the wooden poles or sacred trees used in false worship (these may be posts or trees used in false worship; some scholars link them to the Asherim). God promises to cleanse his people of all idolatry. This verse closes that promise: those who refuse to obey God will face his judgment. Some see it as a prophecy about the time of the Messiah.

For today: do not take lightly the voice of God. Listening to him with humility, letting go of whatever takes his place in your heart, and trusting that he will do justice in the end brings peace, so that you do not have to take revenge yourself.
exp.2:10:
It says that the leaders of Judah were corrupt: the judges took bribes, the priests taught only when they were paid, and the prophets gave messages for money. Even so, they felt secure and said, "The LORD is among us. No disaster can come upon us." The word "divine" here means practicing divination, that is, claiming to announce messages from God.

The speaker is the prophet Micah, sent by God to denounce the injustice of the rulers of Jerusalem. They used religion as a shield, but they oppressed the people. That is why the next verse announces that Jerusalem would be plowed like a field, that is, destroyed.

For today: it is not enough to say that God is with us if we live unjustly or out of self-interest. Let us examine whether at work, in the church, or in the family we act with honesty, without letting money decide what is right.
exp.1:2:
God says that He is also planning against this nation, and the planned action is a disaster. The people who were doing wrong will not be able to free their necks from it, like an animal bound under a heavy yoke. They will no longer walk so proudly, with their heads held high, because a time of calamity is coming.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Micah. The powerful people of Israel planned injustices at night and carried them out by day, taking houses and lands from the weakest. God responds with justice: just as they planned evil, He plans a punishment that fits what they have done.

For today: God sees what we plan in secret, not only what we do. If we have any power, great or small, let us use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them. Humility and justice protect us from pride.
exp.0:9:
It says the disaster is so great that it should not be reported in Gath, a Philistine city, so that the enemies will not celebrate. Nor should people weep out loud; instead they should humble themselves and roll in the dust, an ancient sign of mourning. Beth-leaphrah means "house of dust," a play on words.

The prophet Micah, a messenger of God, speaks around the eighth century BC. He announces judgment for the people's injustice and idolatry. The wound reaches as far as Judah and Jerusalem. The phrase may recall David's lament in 2 Samuel 1:20, though scholars do not all agree on this with the same certainty.

For today: when sin brings pain, do not disguise it or boast about it. Humble yourself before God, weep with sincerity, and ask for his mercy. And do not rejoice when others fall.
exp.4:4:
He says that the Messiah announced in the preceding verses will be our peace. If Assyria invades our land and tramples our citadels, God will raise up leaders to defend the people, enough of them to answer the threat. "Seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men" is a numerical expression that suggests abundance: more than enough.

The prophet Micah speaks in a time of Assyrian threat. The promise comes from the announcement of a ruler born in Bethlehem (5:2). Many Christians see Jesus here as the source of peace. Scholars debate whether Assyria refers only to the historical empire or also symbolizes God's enemies in general.

For today: when a threat feels greater than you can handle, remember that God provides what is needed, often through other people. Trust in Christ as your peace and seek support in your community of faith.
exp.1:7:
It says that God's own people, who used to be his, now act as his enemy. They strip the splendid robe right off unsuspecting passersby, as if they were soldiers coming home from battle and taking the spoils. The "robe" in the verse is the fine outer garment that a person wears. "Unsuspecting" means the travelers have no reason to expect trouble and are not on guard. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and some translations understand it a little differently.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. The powerful of Israel were taking advantage of ordinary people, taking their possessions, and even wanting to silence the prophet who rebuked them. God reminds them that his words do good to those who walk uprightly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, at work, in business, or in the family, we take advantage of someone weaker. God sees injustice and calls us to look after others instead of profiting from them.
exp.2:11:
Because of the sins of Judah's leaders, Zion will be plowed like a field, Jerusalem will become a heap of rubble, and the temple mount will become a wooded ridge.

The prophet Micah speaks for God around the end of the eighth century B.C. He accuses judges, priests, and prophets of using their positions to get rich and to act unjustly, while they kept saying, "Is not the Lord among us?" They believed the temple would protect them, even though they were living wickedly. Jeremiah 26:18 recalls that this warning moved King Hezekiah to seek God.

For today: God is not fooled by a religion that is only for show. Let us ask him to examine our hearts, and let us live with honesty and justice, not only with words of faith.
exp.3:5:
He says that God himself will gather his weak and wounded people. The one who is "lame" is the person who walks with difficulty, and the "outcast" is the one who has been cast away or pushed out. The verse also speaks of those whom God "afflicted," that is, those he allowed to suffer. The words for "assemble" and "gather" are the language of a shepherd who brings his scattered sheep together.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. The people of Israel would be taken into exile because of their sin, but God promises to restore them. After announcing this rescue, the text speaks of a remnant who will become a strong nation, with the Lord reigning in Zion. Many Christians see here a hope that points to the reign of Christ; others read it mainly as a promise for Israel.

If you feel wounded, tired, or set apart, God does not see you as a burden. He seeks out the weak and gathers them. Come to him with confidence, and at the same time be someone who welcomes and cares for others who are walking with difficulty.
exp.4:9:
And it will happen in that day, declares the LORD, that I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots.

The explanation says that God, in "that day" the prophet announces, will take away the horses and war chariots of his people. The phrase "I will remove" means to take away or eliminate, and the chariots are the battle chariots, the great military strength of that time.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Micah. Earlier, he promises that the remnant of Jacob will be strong and will defeat its enemies. Now he makes clear that this victory will not come from weapons or armies, but from Him. For this reason he also removes fortresses and sorcery, everything the people had placed their trust in. Some believe he is speaking of the time of the Messiah, and others of a purification that is near; the text does not specify.

For today: ask yourself where you have placed your security, whether in money, plans, or influence. God may remove those supports to teach you to trust in Him.
exp.0:8:
The prophet says that Samaria's wound cannot be healed, and that this injury did not stay there but spread on to Judah. It has reached the very gate of Jerusalem, the city of God's people. The wound is serious, and in this verse "incurable" means there is no cure for it.

The prophet Micah speaks on God's behalf. He has just announced judgment on Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, because of its idolatry. Now he warns that Judah is not safe, since its sin is much like Samaria's. For this reason Micah mourns and weeps. Scholars believe this points to the Assyrian invasions of that time, though the text does not give every detail.

For today: let us not think that sin is only someone else's problem. If we tolerate small idolatries in the heart, the harm can reach our own doorstep. Let us ask God to examine us and to bring us to repentance in time.
exp.1:12:
One who breaks open the way will go up before them. He is like someone who knocks down a wall or a closed gate so that others can get out. Then the people will break through the gate and go out by it. Their King will pass through before them, with the LORD as their leader.

The prophet Micah speaks in God's name to a people who had fallen into injustice and false promises. In the verse before, God promises to gather the rest of Israel like sheep into their fold. Here he presents this as a king who guides and delivers his people. Some Christians see in the one who breaks open the way an image of Christ; others understand it first as a promise of return from exile. Both readings have been held.

For today: when you feel shut in by problems or fears, remember that God does not send you alone. He goes ahead, opens the way, and invites you to follow him with confidence.
exp.4:12:
God says he will destroy the carved images and the sacred pillars that stood among his people. The "carved images" are figures cut from wood or stone, and the "sacred pillars" are stones or columns set up for worship. The promise that the people "will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands" means they will stop worshiping what they themselves had made.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. In this passage he promises to cleanse his people of idolatry, sorcery, and trust in fortresses. Some understand this as a purification after judgment, and others see in it also a promise for the time of the Messiah, announced in this same chapter.

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by our own hands take the place of God: money, success, image, or security. Let us ask him to free us from them and to trust in him alone.
exp.2:4:
This is what the LORD says about the prophets who lead my people astray. They proclaim peace while they have something to chew on, but if someone puts nothing into their mouths, they declare war against that person. "Lead astray" means to cause people to wander off course. "Declare war" means they announce or prepare an attack.

Micah speaks for the LORD in a time of injustice in Judah and Israel. The leaders were oppressing the people, and these prophets shaped their message to suit their own gain. That is why God says that he will bring their visions to an end: there will be no revelation or answer for them.

Today it invites us to examine whom we listen to and why. A true message is not sold or adjusted to money or applause. If we teach or guide others, let us seek to please God and to speak the truth with love.
exp.1:10:
It says that if a man came along who was all wind, empty and without truth, and spoke falsely, promising "I will preach to you of wine and strong drink" (an abundance of drink and pleasure), he would be just the preacher this people wanted. The phrase "a man of wind" points to someone whose words have no substance behind them.

Here Micah speaks, denouncing the powerful people of Judah who oppressed women and children and seized homes. The people rejected messages of judgment and wanted preachers who spoke of comfort. It is an irony: they preferred a charlatan over a true messenger of God. Then comes a promise of rescue.

For today: let us examine whether we seek messages that only flatter us or the truth that corrects and heals us. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and ask God for a humble heart willing to change.
exp.2:0:
It says that God, through the prophet, calls the attention of Israel's leaders and rulers. He asks them whether knowing what is just was not their duty. The word "hear" in the verse is the one the explanation refers to, and "justice" is the key idea. "Should you not know justice" means "wasn't it your responsibility to know what is right."
