The speaker is Micah, a prophet of the eighth century B.C., who delivers God's message. He speaks to the leaders of the people, who had the responsibility of administering justice. The verses that follow show that they were doing the opposite: they hated good and mistreated the people, using harsh images of flesh and bones to describe their abuse.

For today: if you have any authority, at home, at work, or in the church, remember that God expects you to use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them. Ask Him for wisdom to act justly.
exp.6:12:
The explanation says that the earth itself will be left desolate, laid waste and in ruins, as a result of what its inhabitants have done. "Desolate" means emptied and wrecked. "Inhabitants" refers to the people who live there.

Micah is the prophet who speaks. The verses before this one announce the restoration of Israel: walls rebuilt and people returning from many places. This verse makes a contrast: while God restores his people, the earth suffers the consequences of its inhabitants' deeds. Some scholars think it refers to the nations, others to the land of Israel itself; the text does not fully make this clear. Immediately afterward the prophet prays that God will shepherd his people.

Our choices have real consequences. Today we can ask ourselves what we are sowing with our actions, and turn to God, who forgives and restores those who return to him.
exp.3:9:
God tells Jerusalem, called "Daughter of Zion," that she will suffer like a woman in labor. She will have to leave the city, camp out in the open fields and go as far as Babylon. But right there the LORD will rescue her and redeem her, that is, buy back her freedom, from the hand of her enemies.

The one speaking is the prophet Micah, announcing God's message. The verses before and after speak of enemies surrounding Jerusalem. Micah announces that there will be an exile, and that God will not abandon his people there. He mentions Babylon, which later became the place of the exile. Scholars agree that this is a prophecy of that time, though they debate how it relates to the future.

For today: when you go through a pain that feels like exile, remember that God can work even there. Bring him your anguish honestly and trust that he is still your deliverer.
exp.1:9:
The passage tells the people to get up and leave, because this land is no longer a place of rest. The word "rest" here means peace and calm, the security of living safely in one's home. The land is defiled, that is, stained by sin, and its defilement brings destruction, a grievous destruction.

Here God speaks through the prophet Micah. The powerful in Israel were oppressing their own people: they stripped the clothing from others, drove women out of their homes, and robbed the children. Because of this injustice, God announces that they will lose the land where they felt secure. Many understand this to refer to the exile that was coming.

For today: we cannot live at peace while we tolerate injustice. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are taking advantage of others in any way, and ask God to correct us and help us to treat everyone with justice and mercy.
exp.5:9:
God asks whether treasures gained through wickedness are still kept in the house of the wicked, along with a short ephah, a dry measure that gives less than it should and that He calls accursed. The one called "wicked" is someone who lives without respect for God. A short ephah is a measure that gives the buyer less than what is fair, in order to cheat them.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. He has just said what He requires: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with Him. Now He accuses the city, which was getting rich through false measures, deceit, and lies. Its worship did not match the way it treated others.

For today: check whether you are honest in everyday life, such as at work, in prices, in debts, and in what you promise. God is concerned with justice in money, not only with what we sing or pray.
exp.1:11:
God promises to gather all of you, the people of Jacob, that is, Israel, and to collect those who remain after the punishment. He describes them as sheep brought together into a pen, like a flock gathered within its pasture. The "noisy throng" is the sound and bustle of a large crowd brought back together once more.

Here God speaks through the prophet Micah. Earlier he had denounced the injustice and false sense of security of the people, who preferred prophets who promised wine and comfort. Now, in the midst of judgment, a promise of rescue appears. Interpreters debate whether it speaks of the return from exile, of a future hope, or of both.

For today: even if you have failed or feel scattered, God remains a shepherd who gathers and cares. Return to Him with confidence, and also seek out other believers to walk together with.
exp.0:10:
The explanation says that the inhabitants of Shaphir, whose name sounds like "beautiful," will be driven away in shameful nakedness. The people of Zaanan will not come out, because they are afraid. Beth-ezel mourns and can no longer give support. The last sentence is hard to read and is understood in several ways.

The prophet Micah speaks, delivering God's message. He uses wordplay with the names of towns in Judah to announce judgment for sin. Many think it refers to an enemy invasion, probably Assyrian, although the text does not give every detail.

For today: do not trust in your good image, your strength, or your secure place. Ask God to show you any hidden sin, and turn back to Him before the consequences arrive.
exp.5:1:
God calls the mountains and the enduring foundations of the earth to listen to his case. An "indictment" is a formal charge or legal accusation, and "argue it" means he will set out his case against Israel. God has a case against his people, and he will bring it before them.

God speaks through the prophet Micah. It is like a courtroom scene where the mountains act as witnesses or the jury. Then God recalls what he did for his people: he brought them out of Egypt and gave them leaders. In this way he shows that Israel has been unfaithful to him, despite all his care.

For today: God does not hide himself or grow angry in silence; he invites us to speak with him honestly. We can ask ourselves whether we have forgotten his goodness, and pray with sincerity, willing to listen to what he wants to tell us.
exp.2:6:
What it says: The prophets who misled the people will be put to shame, and the diviners will be disgraced. They will cover their mouths, a sign of shame, because they will have nothing to say. God will give them no answer.

Context: The prophet Micah speaks for the LORD. He accuses the prophets who promised peace to those who paid them and who threatened those who did not. They bent the message to fit their profit. That is why God takes away their sight, leaving them in darkness. Micah, by contrast, says that he is filled with the Spirit to declare God's justice and to name sin.

For today: Let us examine whom we listen to and what message we seek. A true word from God does not always comfort us; sometimes it corrects us. Let us ask for humility to receive the truth, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.2:2:
He says that Israel's leaders treat the people as if they were food. They eat the flesh of the people, strip off their skin, break their bones, and chop them up like meat for the cooking pot. The image of stripping off their skin is a vivid, figurative picture of cruel exploitation.

The prophet Micah speaks on God's behalf, addressing the princes and judges of Israel. They were supposed to know and practice justice, but they hated what is good and loved what is evil. With this image, God denounces their abuse of the weakest. The text that follows announces that when they cry out, God will not answer them.

For today: if we have any power, whether at home, at work, or in the church, we should use it to care for people and not to take advantage of them. Let us ask God for a just and compassionate heart.
exp.6:18:
This verse says that God will again show us compassion. The phrase "he will turn again" points to God returning to his people with mercy. The statement that he will vanquish our iniquities means he will overcome them completely and bring them under his control. And the picture of God casting our sins out into the depths of the sea is an image of complete forgiveness: our wrongs are sunk, beyond reach.

The prophet Micah speaks on behalf of the people of Israel. He ends his book with praise, after speaking of judgment and of grief over sin. He trusts that God does not keep his anger forever, because he delights in mercy. He grounds this hope in the promises made to Abraham and Jacob.

For today: if you have already repented, do not keep carrying guilt that God says he has thrown into the sea. Draw near to him with confidence, receive his forgiveness, and walk in freedom.
exp.6:13:
This verse is a prayer. The prophet asks God to care for his people the way a shepherd cares for his flock. The shepherd's staff is the tool he uses to guide and protect the sheep. Your people are described as the flock of God's inheritance, meaning the ones who belong to him. The prophet asks God to let them graze in Bashan and Gilead, fertile regions good for livestock and remembered as a time of plenty.

The one speaking is the prophet Micah, who pleads on behalf of Israel. The people live surrounded by judgment and hardship, but the prophet trusts that God will restore them. The verses that follow show God answering with wonders, such as when he brought his people out of Egypt.

For today: when you feel alone or in need, pray with confidence, as Micah did. Remember what God has done before and ask him to guide you, care for you, and provide for you.
exp.5:12:
God says that He Himself will punish His people. He is the one who will strike them, and the verse states plainly that the punishment is to ruin them because of their sins, so the cause is clear.

The Lord, through the prophet Micah, speaks to the city of Jerusalem and its people. The verses before this one show the sin: false weights, deception, and riches gained through violence and lies. What follows describes the consequences: eating without being satisfied, sowing without reaping. God does not overlook injustice in business.

For today: examine honestly how you handle your money and your work. If you have cheated, even in small things, ask God for forgiveness and make right the harm you have done. He is pleased with those who are just and honest in everyday life.
exp.1:5:
Verse 6 reports that some in Israel told the prophets, "Do not preach!" They wanted to silence those who announced God's message. They said that if the prophets kept preaching, disgrace would overtake them.

Micah speaks to a people who were committing injustices, such as seizing fields and taking advantage of the weakest. Those who heard his warnings of judgment were angered and wanted to silence him. Here Micah quotes the words of these opponents. Some understand that they spoke with contempt toward the prophets and preferred a comfortable message.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we accept that God's Word corrects us or whether we look only for what pleases us. Listening with humility, even when it hurts, leads us to change and to live with justice.

sum.4: Micah announces that Israel will be besieged and humiliated, but from little Bethlehem a ruler will come forth whose origins are from of old, eternal, who will shepherd with the strength of God and bring peace. The remnant of Jacob will be like dew and like a lion among the nations. God will remove the weapons, the sorcery, and the idols from his people.
sum.0: God speaks to Micah, and announces that he will come to judge Samaria and Jerusalem for their rebellion and idolatry. The mountains will melt away, and Samaria will be left in ruins. Micah weeps, because the punishment reaches as far as Judah, and the nearby towns will mourn what is coming.
sum.2: Micah accuses Israel's leaders of hating what is good, oppressing the people, and twisting justice. The prophets and priests teach and give oracles for money, yet they claim that God is with them. God replies that he will not listen to them, and that Jerusalem will be left like a plowed field.
sum.6: Micah laments that the people have become corrupt, and that no one can be trusted anymore, not even friends or family. Even so, he decides to wait on God, acknowledges his own sin, and trusts that God will raise him up. The chapter ends by praising God, who forgives, forgets sin, and keeps his promises.
sum.3: In the last days, Micah announces, the mountain of the LORD will be raised up above all others, and many nations will come to learn His ways. There will be peace, with no more war. God promises to gather His wounded people and to reign over them. Although Zion will suffer, even going as far as Babylon, there God will rescue her and make her strong against her enemies.
sum.1: Micah denounces the powerful people who lie awake at night plotting wickedness, and who, at dawn, seize houses and fields from ordinary people. God announces a punishment for them, but the people reject the prophets who warn them. In the end, God promises to gather the remnant of Israel like a flock, with their King and the LORD leading them at the front.
sum.5: In Micah 6, God brings his people to court and calls them to answer. He reminds them that he brought them up out of Egypt, and he teaches them that he does not want empty sacrifices. Instead, he wants them to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with him. He then rebukes them for deceit and violence, and he announces that they will face consequences for following the wicked ways of Omri and Ahab.
